title: Seneca practiced being poor (on purpose)
sources: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 18 (tr. R. M. Gummere, 1917): days of the cheapest fare and coarse dress, 'Is this the condition that I feared?'
Kahneman & Tversky (1979), Prospect Theory: losses loom larger than gains (often summarized as roughly twice)
Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: what is and is not up to us

scenes.text:
One of Rome's *richest* men
practiced being *poor.*
scenes.say: One of Rome's richest men practiced being poor. On purpose.

scenes.quote: Is this the condition that I feared?
scenes.author: Seneca
scenes.say: He told a friend: spend a few days on the cheapest food and the roughest clothes. Then ask yourself, is this the condition that I feared?

scenes.label: how much harder a loss hits than an equal gain
scenes.say: Modern research says a loss hits about twice as hard as an equal gain.
So the fear is bigger than the loss. Once you know you can live on less, a crash or a bad month loses its grip.

scenes.text:
He wasn't preparing to be *poor.*
He was preparing to be *free.*
scenes.say: He wasn't preparing to be poor. He was preparing to be free.

scenes.text:
Try it for *one day.*
What are you really *afraid* of?
scenes.say: Try it for one day. What are you really afraid of?
